info.description:
# HTML FOR DOCX ![Tests](https://github.com/dfop02/html4docx/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg) [![PyPI Downloads](https://static.pepy.tech/personalized-badge/html-for-docx?period=total&units=INTERNATIONAL_SYSTEM&left_color=BLACK&right_color=GREEN&left_text=downloads)](https://pepy.tech/projects/html-for-docx) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/html-for-docx.svg) ![Supported Versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/html-for-docx.svg) Convert html to docx, this project is a fork from the discontinued [pqzx/html2docx](https://github.com/pqzx/html2docx). ## How to install `pip install html-for-docx` ## Usage #### The basic usage Add HTML-formatted content to an existing `.docx` document ```python from docx import Document from html4docx import HtmlToDocx document = Document('existing_file.docx') parser = HtmlToDocx() html_string = '

Hello world

' parser.add_html_to_document(html_string, document) document.save('existing_file.docx') ``` You can use `python-docx` to manipulate directly the file, here an example ```python from docx import Document from html4docx import HtmlToDocx document = Document() parser = HtmlToDocx() html_string = '

Hello world

' parser.add_html_to_document(html_string, document) document.save('your_file_name.docx') ``` or incrementally add new html to document and save it when finished, new content will always be added at the end ```python from docx import Document from html4docx import HtmlToDocx document = Document() parser = HtmlToDocx() for part in ['First', 'Second', 'Third']: parser.add_html_to_document(f'

{part} Part

', document) parser.save('your_file_name.docx') ``` When you pass a `Document` object, you can either use `document.save()` from python-docx or `parser.save()` from html4docx, both work well. Both support saving it in-memory, using `BytesIO`. ```python from io import BytesIO from docx import Document from html4docx import HtmlToDocx buffer = BytesIO() document = Document() parser = HtmlToDocx() html_string = '

Hello world

' parser.add_html_to_document(html_string, document) # Save the document to the in-memory buffer parser.save(buffer) # If you need to read from the buffer again after saving, # you might need to reset its position to the beginning buffer.seek(0) ``` #### Convert files directly ```python from html4docx import HtmlToDocx parser = HtmlToDocx() parser.parse_html_file(input_html_file_path, output_docx_file_path) # You can also define a encoding, by default is utf-8 parser.parse_html_file(input_html_file_path, output_docx_file_path, 'utf-8') ``` If the HTML file references local images or stylesheets, allow the folder that holds them (see [External resources security](#external-resources-security)): ```python import os parser.options['local-files-root'] = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(input_html_file_path)) parser.parse_html_file(input_html_file_path, output_docx_file_path) ``` #### Convert files from a string ```python from html4docx import HtmlToDocx parser = HtmlToDocx() docx = parser.parse_html_string(input_html_file_string) ``` #### Change table styles Tables are not styled by default. Use the `table_style` attribute on the parser to set a table style before convert html. The style is used for all tables. ```python from html4docx import HtmlToDocx parser = HtmlToDocx() parser.table_style = 'Light Shading Accent 4' docx = parser.parse_html_string(input_html_file_string) ``` To add borders to tables, use the `Table Grid` style: ```python parser.table_style = 'Table Grid' ``` All table styles we support can be found [here](https://python-docx.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/styles-understanding.html#table-styles-in-default-template). ## Options All options are set through `parser.options` before parsing. Copy only the ones you need to change: ```python from html4docx import HtmlToDocx parser = HtmlToDocx() # --- Rendering --- parser.options['images'] = False # Default True. False ignores all images. parser.options['tables'] = False # Default True. False renders only the raw table content. parser.options['styles'] = False # Default True. False ignores all CSS (also disables 'style-map'). parser.options['fix-html'] = False # Default True. False skips BeautifulSoup fixing of missing HTML tags. parser.options['style-map'] = False # Default True. False ignores CSS class to Word style mapping. parser.options['tag-override'] = False # Default True. False ignores HTML tag overrides. parser.options['html-comments'] = True # Default False. True renders "" comments. # --- External resources security (see the section below) --- parser.options['allow-remote-resources'] = False # Default True. False skips all http(s) images and stylesheets. parser.options['private-network-allowlist'] = ["10.0.5.20", "192.168.10.0/24"] # Default []. Private IPs/CIDRs that may be fetched. parser.options['local-files-root'] = '/srv/app/assets' # Default None. Directory local files may be read from (None = disabled). parser.options['max-resource-bytes'] = 5 * 1024 * 1024 # Default 10 MB. Maximum size of each fetched resource. parser.options['allow-private-network'] = False # Default False. True allows EVERY private address and ignores the allowlist: trusted HTML only! docx = parser.parse_html_string(input_html_file_string) ``` ### External resources security HTML is often untrusted input, so images (``) and stylesheets (``) are fetched under a restrictive policy by default: - **Remote resources:** only `http`/`https` are fetched. `file://`, `ftp://` and any other scheme are always refused. Inline images (`data:image/...`) keep working. - **Private network:** requests to non-public addresses (loopback, private ranges, link-local such as the cloud metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`, reserved, multicast) are refused. The check is applied to the IP actually connected to, on every redirect hop, so DNS rebinding and open redirects can't bypass it. - **Local files:** disabled by default. When `local-files-root` is set, only files inside that directory (after resolving `..` and symlinks) can be read, and relative paths are resolved against it. - **Size:** each resource, remote or local, is limited to `max-resource-bytes`. **Reaching an internal server.** Add its addresses to `private-network-allowlist`. Only those IPs/CIDRs are opened, and everything else stays blocked. Public addresses (CDNs, websites) never need to be listed. Keep entries as narrow as possible: a broad range such as `169.254.0.0/16` also opens cloud metadata endpoints. Invalid entries raise `ValueError` instead of being silently ignored. `allow-private-network` opens every private address at once and should only be used when the HTML is fully trusted. > **Converting HTML from users?** Keep `allow-private-network` disabled, keep `private-network-allowlist` as small as possible and never point `local-files-root` at a directory containing sensitive files. If you don't need external images or stylesheets at all, set `allow-remote-resources` to `False`. Blocked or unavailable resources are skipped and a warning is logged (logger `html4docx.resources`); the conversion itself does not fail. #### Migrating from <=1.2.x Public `http`/`https` URLs and `data:image/...` images work as before. What changed: - **Local paths** in `` and `` are disabled by default. Set `local-files-root` to the folder that holds your assets. Relative paths are now resolved against it, not the current working directory: ```python import os parser.options['local-files-root'] = os.path.abspath('./assets') ``` - **Private network addresses** (e.g. an intranet server) are blocked. Add them to `private-network-allowlist`. - **Proxies:** `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` environment variables are ignored, because routing through a proxy would bypass the private network protection. If your server can only reach the internet through a proxy, remote resources will not load. Embed images as `data:image/...` URIs, put CSS in an inline `
